claims.text: Machine-learning models can efficiently predict free energies for high-entropy systems.
Machine-learning models can predict high-temperature thermodynamic properties for high-entropy systems.
Using machine learning would reduce the computational cost and time of the calculations.
The proposed domain includes elemental, binary, and multicomponent systems under the designation of high-entropy systems.
The method would apply to both solid and fluid states.
A machine-learning or surrogate model should be developed to predict free energies and thermodynamic properties.
The proposed method is applicable across high-entropy systems having multiple principal elements and complex phase diagrams.
The proposed method is applicable at temperatures up to several thousand kelvin.
Neural networks trained on available data can serve as the surrogate model.
Random forests trained on available data can serve as the surrogate model.
The model can identify patterns in training data and use them to predict properties of unseen systems.
The model would predict free energies faster than explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation and TOR-TILD.
The model would provide accurate predictions of high-entropy-material properties.
The resulting predictions would enable discovery of materials with desired properties.
Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is accurate but computationally expensive, and TOR-TILD is slow for multicomponent systems.
Model accuracy depends on training-data quality and quantity, model architecture, and hyperparameter choices.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field categorizes elemental and binary systems as high-entropy systems, whereas the conditions and boundary define the target in terms of multiple principal elements. These domain definitions are inconsistent.
